# Installing Git for Windows {#sec-git-windows}

This appendix is for students on **Windows**. It installs [Git for Windows]{.uwred}, which bundles both Git and the Bash shell into a single program called [Git Bash]{.uwred} — the terminal we use throughout these lessons. Plan on about ten minutes, and do it before the live session.

::: {.callout-note}
On **macOS** and **Linux**, Bash is already built in, and Git is usually present too. Open a terminal and run `git --version`. If Git is installed, you'll see a version number and can skip this appendix. On macOS, if it's missing you'll be prompted to install the command line developer tools — accept that (do **not** install the full Xcode).
:::

## Download the installer

Go to [gitforwindows.org](https://gitforwindows.org/) and download the installer. Once it finishes, double-click the downloaded `.exe` to start.

## Run the installer

The installer has many screens. You can accept the [defaults]{.uwred} on nearly all of them — just click **Next** through to the end. Four screens are worth stopping for, because they match how we work in class:

- **Choosing the default editor used by Git** — from the dropdown, select [Use the Nano editor by default]{.uwred}. (You may need to scroll up to find it.) Our lessons write commit messages in nano.
- **Adjusting the name of the initial branch in new repositories** — choose [Override the default branch name]{.uwred} and type `main`. This matches the branch name we use everywhere in these materials.
- **Adjusting your PATH environment** — keep the recommended [Git from the command line and also from 3rd-party software]{.uwred}. If you miss this, Git Bash won't work properly with other tools.
- **Configuring the line ending conversions** — keep [Checkout Windows-style, commit Unix-style line endings]{.uwred}.

For every other screen — OpenSSH, the HTTPS backend, the terminal emulator, credential manager, and so on — the default is fine. Click **Install**, then **Finish**.

## Open Git Bash and check

Open the Start menu, type `Git Bash`, and open it. You'll get a terminal window. Confirm Git is installed:

```bash
git --version
```

```
git version 2.46.0.windows.1
```

A version number means you're set. This Git Bash window gives you [both Git and Bash]{.uwred} — it is the terminal you'll use to follow along in class.

## If Git Bash can't find your home folder

Occasionally `~` (your home folder) isn't set correctly. If commands that use `~` misbehave, open the Windows **Command Prompt** (Start menu → type `cmd`) and run:

```
setx HOME "%USERPROFILE%"
```

You should see `SUCCESS: Specified value was saved.` Close and reopen Git Bash.

## Next steps

With Git Bash installed, you're ready to:

- Set your name and email, covered in the Introduction and Setup unit
- Connect to GitHub, covered in the Setting Up SSH Keys appendix
